article.title: Lula Defeats Bolsonaro - YDSA
article.content: Incumbent Victory Rolls Back Latin America’s Right Wing Wave Incumbent President Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva came ahead in the second round of Brazil’s Presidential election, winning a fourth term for the left-wing Worker’s Party (PT) candidate. The results are 51% for Lula, and 48% for Flavio Bolsonaro , candidate for the Liberal Party (PL) and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. Sunday’s victory is a significant comeback for Lula. When the first round of voting ended on October 4, Bolsonaro was ahead, 47% to Lula’s 45%. Bolsonaro’s lead in the first round of voting sparked massive youth mobilizations across the country as millions of Brazilians assembled in the streets to protest against the far-right candidate. Over a million Brazilians turned out to a rally with Lula in Rio De Janeiro the day before the election. As part of the effort to re-elect Lula, Brazil’s Congress passed a long-awaited end to the 6-day work week on October 14th. The constitutional amendment, which shortens the work week to 40 hours, was sponsored by socialist deputy Erika Hilton, a member of the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL). PSOL campaigned for Lula alongside the PT and led many of the youth mobilizations. Many cited Lula’s age- he is 80 years old- cost of living issues, and security concerns as detrimental to Lula’s campaign. Some polls showed Flavio ahead before Sunday, making Lula’s victory all the more notable. Street mobilizations and the successful legislative push were seen as instrumental to Lula’s upset against Bolsonaro. An electoral breakdown from Sunday night shows Lula leading in 14 Brazilian states, and Flavio in an equal number. Lula performed strongest in Piaui, a state located in Brazil’s northeast, traditionally considered a stronghold for him and the PT, while Flavio did best in Roraima, located in the north. Lula celebrated at his campaign headquarters in Sao Paulo , where his supporters hugged him, applauded, and chanted “Lula, Lula!” “ Today my speech is one of gratitude. We had the lowest number of abstentions and null votes. I want to thank the generosity of the Brazilian people and the Brazilian youth who took to the streets ,” said Lula in a speech to his supporters, according to reporting from Ricardo Noblat. Lula’s victory is globally significant, representing the first break in a series of right-wing victories that shook Latin America since US President Donald J. Trump returned to office. It was also widely felt that the fate of the Amazon rainforest, commonly referred to as the “ Lungs of the Earth ” for its role in capturing carbon from the atmosphere, was at stake in this election. Deforestation surged under Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency before dropping to the lowest level in over a decade during Lula’s current term. Despite Lula’s electoral success, numerous obstacles remain. Nationally, PL, Bolsonaro’s party, controls both chambers of Brazil’s Congress along with numerous governorships. Internationally, there is the threat of U.S. intervention, especially as the US military captured and deposed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year. Although he hasn’t endorsed a candidate, President Donald Trump has praised Flavio Bolsonaro, describing him as a “ A smart young man who loves his Country ,” in a Truth Social post from June 2nd. Sanctions were imposed against Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes , who led investigations into Bolsonaro’s coup plot. All of which lent weight to Flavio Bolsonaro’s rejection of the election results. Speaking to his supporters , Flavio refused to concede. “It is impossible to recognize the election results,” he said. “we will use our legal team, we will request the annulment of these elections.” An investigation from Reuters released on October 24 revealed that Darren Beattie, a US Senior Advisor ‌for Western Hemisphere Affairs, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor at the State Department, instructed diplomats that it was “ US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader.” None of this dampened the mood of Lula supporters Sunday night, with footage of celebrations from Lula and Worker’s Party voters filling social media. “This is a huge win for the Brazilian working class,” said James Hernández, YDSA co-chair who observed the election results with members of the DSA International Commission. “Students and youth really mobilized over the last three weeks to ensure we don’t go back to Bolsonaro.” Hernández states that Lula’s win is not only a victory for Brazil, but “for the international working class, for Latin America. This represents a resistance to fascism. I’m excited, and I think everybody should be hyped.” YDSA National Co-Chair James Hernández alongside DSA congressional candidate Chris Rabb and other members of the DSA-IC’s delegation to Brazil.
